provisioning: Farmers had to feed people who did other work. This model illustrates the paper’s relationships between community size, location and a constructed production index. Community size reorganizes a fixed illustrative population; distance associations are calculated separately. The controls cannot establish how much rice a ruler could collect.
relocation: People may prefer another centre when food or opportunities worsen at home. Elites and workers can move under different rules; farmers stay attached to their fields. Outside opportunities, portable wealth and moving hurdles are assumptions. Compare movement with movement blocked before interpreting a court’s departure.
petri: Food production supports households and public commitments. Collecting more food can fund maintenance while leaving less with households; reserves can provide relief. The model adds growth, migration and recurring costs to a paper-inspired coordination assumption. Its droughts and institutional rates are invented experiments.
monsoon: A tree-ring drought record changes agricultural conditions through an assumed crop-response rule. Compare the same sampled society with neutral climate. The crop-response choices represent uncertainty in our translation, rather than rainfall a government can choose. Activity in the core combines court presence and regional population.
cambodia: Children can attend school and work at the same time. This model asks how school costs, what school offers, enforcement, the credential floor and migration change that balance. The reference has no added programme and keeps the Thailand route open. Programme strengths are assumed, and rural school retention needs an unexplained adjustment. A change here is a scenario result, not an estimated policy impact.
china: Graduates compete for jobs while some wait outside the labour force. The model combines graduate supply, job demand and access through networks. The reference was fitted to the displayed record; some mechanisms remain assumed. Changing a slider explores alternative explanations. The official unemployment definition also changes in 2024.
teachers: Teachers enter through training and hiring and leave through quits or retirement. Training takes time, so a response today may arrive after a shortage begins. The starting workforce is synthetic. Demand growth and departure rates are scenarios, not forecasts for a named country.
angkor: Harvests depend on assumed yield and waterworks condition, and population responds to those harvests. This older experiment has no annual grain ledger and can overspend its military and building budgets. Use its curves to inspect those rules. The displayed population is not a calibrated reconstruction.
campaign: An army takes people away from farming and needs food while travelling. Rice, fish, farm work and construction compete over seasons. The court collects after the village reserve. Routes, transport performance and capture rates are illustrative; stores have no physical cap, which can hide food pressure.
signalling: A supplier sees stone monuments and elephants and decides whether to send tribute. Compare that decision with an observer who knows actual military capacity. Building uses resources that could support a response. The audience’s beliefs and the revenue recovery schedule are assumptions.
obligations: Local food and outside deliveries must pay ritual and court costs. Two consecutive unpaid court bills trigger departure by assumption. A separate rule permits a funded return. Signalling settings can supply pledge decisions here; food ledgers remain separate.
mandala: Compare stored histories from a synthetic map. The reference fails to make Angkor the leading centre and reaches an unmatched population scale. Scenario differences help diagnose model rules. They cannot explain Angkor’s historical geography.
credentials: Students may value a credential for earnings, relative position or access through relationships. These stored comparisons test bundles against different country targets. Target coverage differs by country, so acceptance rates cannot rank the truth of each theory across countries. Selecting a bundle highlights existing results.
institutions: Households, temples and elites receive different shares of harvest. Temple reserves can relieve food shortages under an assumed rule. Each scenario has only one trial. Land rights are recorded without changing harvest, and court and elite stores accumulate without spending.
flight: People can move into a refuge instead of disappearing from the population account. Relief and abstract movement barriers change who remains under state control. Fortress settings bundle labour costs, exit barriers and recapture; this older version does not track refuge food production.
maintenance: Canals need continuing work. Here maintenance falls to 35% of its reference level from year 55. The reshuffle also changes extraction, relief and trust. Compare the maintenance-only case first. Harvest still ignores the remaining farm workforce in this version.
accounts: People divide work among fields and public services. Court stores pay service rations, and the refuge has its own food account. Every year balances food, labour and population. Rates remain hypothetical; there are no battles or frontier supply chains. More military service can redistribute food without proving military success.
cohort: A planner’s first question about a school system is how many entrants finish it. This reconstructed cohort follows 1,000 Grade 1 entrants with constant repetition and dropout rates and counts the pupil-years spent on each graduate. The reference rates are stylised; replace them with rates from your own enrolment data.
sector: A sector plan sets targets for intake, repetition, dropout and class size, then asks what they cost. This simulation moves a stylised six-grade primary system to its targets by 2035 and compares the cost with the money the budget frame provides. An unaffordable plan still runs, so the financing gap is the warning.
schoolmap: Building a school shortens some children’s walks and not others. This micro-planning tool adds schools one at a time to a synthetic district of sixty villages, either where each new school most reduces total walking or in the largest unserved village. Compare the two rules before deciding which villages come first.
lays: Time in school is not the same as learning. Learning-adjusted years discount expected schooling by a harmonised test score, and learning poverty counts children who cannot read with comprehension at the end of primary, including those out of school. Compare adding years with improving what each year teaches.
absorption: Producing graduates is only half of external efficiency; the economy also has to open jobs for them. This balance sheet compares graduates with graduate-job openings from growth and replacement, and tracks a queue of those not yet absorbed. Open the China graduate-queue world to see wages and firms’ choices.
